title: Kingdom of Lysimachus
capsule: Lysimachus was one of Alexander the Great's Macedonian bodyguards (somatophylakes) who received Thrace as his satrapy at the Partition of Triparadisus in 320 BCE and progressively expanded to claim the title of king in 305. He annexed western Asia Minor and much of Macedonia after the Battle of Ipsus (301 BCE) eliminated Antigonus, making his kingdom one of the largest Hellenistic successor states spanning the northern Aegean, Thrace, and Asia Minor to the Taurus. His reign ended at the Battle of Corupedium in 281 BCE, where he was defeated and killed by Seleucus I Nicator; his territories rapidly fragmented, with Asia Minor eventually absorbed by the Seleucid and Pergamene kingdoms.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. The broad territorial outline of Lysimachus's kingdom is documented in Diodorus, Plutarch, and Justin; precise frontier delineations in Thrace and Asia Minor are approximate, reconstructed from narrative accounts of campaigns.
